meta.blurb: Kofi gets the hiccups in a museum, and a fossil expert tells him that his body is full of old parts. Follow his jaw, his ears, his hands and even his hiccups back through hundreds of millions of years to the first fish.
meta.bible: Kofi: a ten-year-old boy with a bad case of the hiccups, curious and a little funny. Dr Adjoa: a kind fossil scientist who works at the Museum of Natural History and loves bones. They walk through the museum halls in one afternoon, from the Fish Hall to the Hall of Mammals. Key terms: Fossil, Fossils, Vertebrate, Vertebrates, Backbone, Skull, Skeleton, Gill, Gills, Arch, Arches, Jaw, Jaws, Lamprey, Shark, Sharks, Denticles, Embryo, Embryos, Fin, Fins, Limb, Limbs, Humerus, Radius, Ulna, Tiktaalik, Tetrapod, Tetrapods, Acanthostega, Amphibian, Amphibians, Reptile, Reptiles, Mammal, Mammals, Lung, Lungs, Lungfish, Swim bladder, Nerve, Nerves, Laryngeal, Giraffe, Hox, Zebrafish, Pax6, Cones, Primates, Receptors, Hammer, Anvil, Stirrup, Eardrum, Goosebumps, Hiccups, Tadpole, Tadpoles, Coccyx, Yolk, Evolution, Ancestor, Ancestors, Radioactive, Cambrian, Devonian, Haeckel, Fish Hall. Facts: the first animals with backbones were small fish-like creatures more than 500 million years ago; Tiktaalik lived about 375 million years ago and its fossils come from Arctic Canada; the first four-legged animals appear about 365 million years ago; about seven in ten human genes have a counterpart in the zebrafish; humans have about 400 working smell genes. Where scientists are not sure, the text says so, especially for the cause of Hiccups. Voice: playful, clear and wondering; the science is real and hedged where it is uncertain; no invented numbers, studies or quotes.

beats.scene: Kofi hiccups loudly in front of a tall glass museum door
beats.summary: Kofi gets the hiccups in a museum, and Dr Adjoa says even hiccups have a story.

beats.scene: Dr Adjoa and Kofi stand beneath a vast skeleton in the main hall
beats.summary: Dr Adjoa explains that all animals with backbones are relatives with a shared ancestry.

beats.scene: Kofi studies a cabinet full of rocks, bones, shells and a microscope
beats.summary: Scientists learn about the past from fossils, living bodies, embryos and DNA.

beats.scene: Different finches and beetles line a long museum shelf under bright lights
beats.summary: Evolution works because bodies vary, some variations help, and helpful ones are passed on.

beats.scene: A rock split open shows the stone outline of a small ancient fish
beats.summary: Fossils form when remains turn to stone, and deeper rock layers are usually older.

beats.scene: A scientist holds a rock sample beside a glowing atom diagram
beats.summary: Radioactive atoms decay at a steady rate, and scientists use them as clocks to date rocks.

beats.scene: A tiny jawless fish swims through dim green water above the seabed
beats.summary: The first animals with backbones were small fish-like creatures more than 500 million years ago.

beats.scene: Kofi presses a hand to his spine beside a glowing fish skeleton
beats.summary: Our spine and skull are inherited from those early fish.

beats.scene: Fish and human skeletons stand side by side in a bright hall
beats.summary: A fish and a person have the same basic plan: skull, spine and ribs.

beats.scene: A lamprey with a round toothed mouth clings to a rock in a tank
beats.summary: Lampreys are living jawless fish that show what early vertebrates were like.

beats.scene: A diagram of bony curved bars supporting the gills along a fish's head
beats.summary: In early fish, curved bars called gill arches held up the gills.

beats.scene: A model shows one gill arch growing bigger and hinging into a mouth
beats.summary: In some early fish the front gill arches became hinged jaws.

beats.scene: A shark's open mouth shows rows of teeth beside a rough patch of skin
beats.summary: Teeth probably began as tough scales in the skin, like a shark's skin denticles.

beats.scene: A shark skeleton of soft grey cartilage hangs beside a stiff white bone
beats.summary: Sharks have skeletons of cartilage, and every baby starts with much cartilage that turns to bone.

beats.scene: A tiny human embryo shows small folds on its neck under soft light
beats.summary: Human embryos form folds in the neck, called arches, that become the jaw, ear and throat.

beats.scene: A glowing tube heart folds into a curve inside a tiny embryo
beats.summary: A human heart starts as a simple tube that loops and divides into four chambers.

beats.scene: Three heart diagrams show two, three and four chambers in a row
beats.summary: Fish hearts have two chambers, amphibians three and mammals four.

beats.scene: A fish's head diagram shows nerves running through each gill arch
beats.summary: Nerves in our head and neck follow the paths first laid down in fish.

beats.scene: A giraffe lowers its long neck beside a diagram of a looping nerve
beats.summary: A nerve to the voice box loops down and back up the neck of a giraffe, an old detour.

beats.scene: A glowing pair of lungs sits inside a diagram of a fish's body
beats.summary: Lungs began in early bony fish, and the swim bladder of many fish came from them.

beats.scene: A lungfish lifts its head to gulp air at a muddy pond
beats.summary: Some living fish, such as lungfish, can breathe air with their lungs.

beats.scene: A fish's side shows a faint line of tiny hair cells along its body
beats.summary: Fish sense water movement with hair cells that are related to those in our inner ear.

beats.scene: Kofi tilts his head beside a drawing of three fluid-filled ear loops
beats.summary: Our balance organs, the three loops of the inner ear, are very like a fish's.

beats.scene: A rainbow of coloured light falls on a fish's eye in clear water
beats.summary: Ancient fish saw in four colours, most mammals lost two, and primates regained a third.

beats.scene: A dog's nose and a human nose above a wall of smell bottles
beats.summary: Humans have about 400 working smell genes, a sign of a longer sense of smell in our ancestors.

beats.scene: A fish's fin and a human arm drawn on a table with matching colours
beats.summary: Fish fins contain the same pattern of bones as a human arm: one, two, then many.

beats.scene: Sunlit green plants and small insects crowd the muddy edge of a shallow pool
beats.summary: Land had food, and shallow water was crowded and low in oxygen, so life on land may have paid off.

beats.scene: A fish with strong fins rests its head on a rock in a stream
beats.summary: A fossil fish called Tiktaalik, about 375 million years old, had a neck and strong fin bones.

beats.scene: Tiktaalik turns its flat head while its body rests in the shallows
beats.summary: Unlike most fish, Tiktaalik could move its head separately from its body: a neck.

beats.scene: An early four-legged animal with many toes crawls from a swamp pool
beats.summary: The first four-legged animals, tetrapods, appeared about 365 million years ago.

beats.scene: A hand with five fingers is outlined over the bones of an early limb
beats.summary: Many early tetrapods had more than five fingers; our five come from a long line of change.

beats.scene: A fly and a person stand beside matching coloured bands along their bodies
beats.summary: Hox genes lay out the body from head to tail in flies, fish and people.

beats.scene: A small striped zebrafish swims in a lab tank under a magnifying lens
beats.summary: About seven in ten human genes have a counterpart in the zebrafish, which scientists use to study the body.

beats.scene: A fly's eye and a human eye are shown with the same glowing gene
beats.summary: A related gene, Pax6, helps to build eyes in flies, fish and people.

beats.scene: A frog sits on a lily pad while a tadpole wriggles below it
beats.summary: Amphibians such as frogs keep a link with water; they lay eggs in water and breathe partly through the skin.

beats.scene: A tough-shelled egg cracks open to show a baby reptile inside
beats.summary: Reptiles evolved eggs with membranes and shells that could be laid on land.

beats.scene: A reptile-like fossil skull shows a jaw made of many separate bones
beats.summary: Early mammal relatives had jaws made of several bones, which later became smaller.

beats.scene: A diagram shows three tiny ear bones named hammer, anvil and stirrup
beats.summary: In mammals, two old jaw bones became ear bones; together with the stirrup, they carry sound.

beats.scene: A furry mammal feeds its young in a nest in a quiet museum diorama
beats.summary: Only mammals have hair and make milk, features that began in their early ancestors.

beats.scene: Kofi's arm with raised hairs and goosebumps in the cool museum air
beats.summary: Goosebumps are a reflex from furry ancestors that raised their fur for warmth or to look big.

beats.scene: A tadpole breathes with feathery gills while a frog swallows air nearby
beats.summary: One idea says hiccups come from a reflex used by tadpoles, but scientists are not sure.

beats.scene: A tiny human embryo with a curved tail beside a tailbone drawing
beats.summary: Early in pregnancy a human embryo has a tail, which shrinks and leaves the tailbone.

beats.scene: A broken egg yolk is drawn above a strand of damaged DNA
beats.summary: People carry a broken copy of a yolk gene, a trace of egg-laying ancestors.

beats.scene: A person with a hand on the lower back sits upright on a bench
beats.summary: Walking upright puts old bones to a new use, which helps explain why backs and knees often hurt.

beats.scene: A sandwich beside a diagram of crossing tubes in a throat
beats.summary: Air and food share the throat, so food sometimes goes down the wrong way.

beats.scene: An old drawing of embryos sits beside a modern scan of real ones
beats.summary: Old drawings of embryos exaggerated the likeness, but the real similarities are still true.

beats.scene: A branching tree of animals is drawn across a long museum wall
beats.summary: All backbone animals fit on one family tree, and DNA agrees with the fossils.

beats.scene: A scientist brushes dust from a fossil bone in a bright field camp
beats.summary: New fossils keep being found, and science keeps testing and improving the story.

beats.scene: Kofi opens his hand wide and studies his fingers in the light
beats.summary: Kofi looks at his hand and thinks of the fins, bones and fish that came before.

beats.scene: Kofi and Dr Adjoa stand quietly at the glass doors as the sun sets
beats.summary: Kofi's hiccups finally stop, and he leaves understanding that his body is a living museum.

B1B2: Kofi has been hiccuping since lunch, and the sound echoes through the museum hall. Dr Adjoa, a fossil scientist, smiles and says that even hiccups have a very old story behind them.
Dr Adjoa tells Kofi that every animal with a backbone is a distant relative of every other one. Fish, frogs, birds, cats and people all share ancestors from long ago.
How can anyone know about animals that died so long ago? Scientists study fossils, compare living bodies, watch how embryos grow and read DNA, and the clues usually agree.
Dr Adjoa explains how evolution works, and it is quite simple. Animals vary a little, those with helpful traits have more young, and so those traits become common.
A fossil forms when the remains of a dead animal are buried in mud and slowly turn to stone. In a stack of rock layers, the deeper ones are usually the older ones.
Some atoms in rocks are radioactive, and they change into other atoms at a steady, known speed. By measuring how much has changed, scientists can work out how old a rock is.
More than 500 million years ago, the first animals with backbones appeared in the sea. They were small, soft fish-like creatures with no jaws and no arms or legs.
Kofi touches his back and feels the bumps of his spine. Dr Adjoa tells him that this row of bones, and the skull that protects his brain, came to him from those first fish.
In the Fish Hall, a fish skeleton stands next to a human one. Both have a skull, a spine and ribs, though the fish has fins instead of arms and legs.
Dr Adjoa shows Kofi a lamprey in a tank. It is a living fish with a round mouth and no jaw, and it looks a little like the early fish from long ago.
Fish breathe with gills, which take oxygen from the water. Curved bars of bone or soft cartilage, called gill arches, hold the gills in place on each side of the head.
Over a very long time, the front gill arches of some early fish grew larger and bent into hinged jaws. Fish with jaws could bite, hunt and chew, and they spread across the seas.
A shark's skin is covered with tiny hard scales called denticles. Scientists think that teeth began as scales like these and moved into the mouth.
A shark's skeleton is made of cartilage, which is firm but bendy, instead of hard bone. Your nose and ears are made of cartilage too, and a baby's skeleton starts with a lot of it.
A few weeks after life begins, a human embryo has little folds in its neck, like gill arches. They are not gills, and they grow into parts of the jaw, ear and throat.
A baby's heart begins as a simple tube that pumps blood. It then bends and divides into four chambers, but a fish's heart has only two.
A fish heart has two chambers, a frog heart has three, and a mammal heart has four. The extra chambers keep oxygen-rich blood apart from used blood, which helps warm-blooded animals stay active.
In fish, nerves run from the brain to each gill arch. In people, many of the same nerves still follow those old paths, even though the arches have become other parts.
A nerve to a giraffe's voice box runs down its neck, loops around a blood vessel, and climbs back up. The detour is several metres long and seems very strange.
Lungs first appeared in early bony fish, which could gulp air. The swim bladder, a gas bag that helps many modern fish float, came later and developed from those lungs.
Lungfish live in rivers that sometimes dry up, and they can breathe air with their lungs. They show how a fish could stay alive when the water was poor in oxygen.
Fish have a line of tiny hair cells along their sides that feel movements in the water. The hair cells in our inner ear, which help us hear and balance, are close relatives of these.
Deep inside your ear, three small fluid-filled loops tell your brain which way your head is moving. Fish have a similar system, and ours is built to the same old plan.
Ancient fish had four kinds of colour-sensing cells in their eyes. Most mammals lost two kinds, but our primate ancestors gained a third kind back, so we see red, green and blue.
People have about 400 working genes for smell, while mice have more than 1,000. Our sense of smell is still very good, but we have lost many of the genes that our ancestors used.

The bones in a fish's front fin follow a pattern: one large bone, then two, then many small ones. Your arm has the same pattern, with one upper arm bone, two forearm bones and many small wrist and finger bones.
Why did some fish begin to leave the water? Scientists think that shallow pools were crowded and short of oxygen, while the land offered plants, insects and fewer enemies.
Tiktaalik was a large fish that lived about 375 million years ago, and its fossils come from Arctic Canada. It had a flat head, a neck and strong fins with bones like a wrist.
Most fish have no neck, so they must turn the whole body to look at something. Tiktaalik could move its head on its own, which was useful when it hunted in shallow water.
The first animals with four legs, called tetrapods, appeared about 365 million years ago. Some of them, such as Acanthostega, still lived mostly in the water, and they had eight fingers on each hand.
Early tetrapods tried different numbers of fingers, and only later did five become common. Almost all land animals with limbs are descended from ones with five or fewer.
Hox genes are a family of genes that mark out the body plan from head to tail. Flies, fish and people all use them, which shows how old and important they are.
About seven in every ten human genes have a matching gene in the zebrafish. Because its babies are clear, scientists can watch the heart, blood and nerves grow.
A gene called Pax6 helps to build eyes in many different animals, from flies to people. Fly eyes and human eyes look nothing alike, yet they depend on the same master switch.
Frogs still live a kind of double life in water and on land. They begin as tadpoles that breathe with gills, and as adults they breathe with lungs and through their skin.
Later, some animals evolved eggs with a tough shell and protective membranes. These eggs can be laid on dry land, so the babies no longer need a pond.
The jaw of a reptile has several bones, while the human jaw has only one. Fossils of early mammal relatives show some of those bones becoming smaller over time.
Your middle ear holds three tiny bones, named the hammer, the anvil and the stirrup. Two of them came from the jaw of an ancestor and now carry sound to the inner ear.
Mammals are the only animals with real hair, and mothers feed their babies with milk. These features are signs of our early mammal ancestors, who were small and often active at night.
When Kofi feels cold, tiny muscles lift the hairs on his arms and make goosebumps. In furry animals this fluffs the fur to keep warm or to look bigger, but in people it does very little.
Now Kofi's hiccups come back, as loud as before. Some scientists think that hiccups come from a reflex that helps tadpoles breathe with their gills, but no one has proved it.
Early in pregnancy, a human embryo has a short tail. It shrinks away, and what remains is a small group of bones at the bottom of the spine, called the coccyx.
Birds and reptiles make egg yolk with a certain gene. We carry a broken copy of a similar gene, which no longer works, as a trace of ancestors who laid eggs.
Our spine was shaped over a very long time in animals that walked on four legs. Walking upright is a fairly new use for it, and that may be one reason why backs and knees so often hurt.
Your windpipe and your food pipe cross in the throat, which is why food sometimes goes down the wrong way. This odd design is another leftover from our fish ancestors.

In the 1800s, Ernst Haeckel drew embryos in a way that made them look more alike than they really are. Modern scientists have shown that early embryos do share features, but they do not replay the whole history of their ancestors.
Scientists can draw one big family tree for all animals with backbones. The tree built from DNA agrees well with the tree built from fossils, which gives us confidence in both.
Fossil hunters keep finding new fossils, and each one can add to the story or change it. Some details about our ancient ancestors are still uncertain, and scientists are happy to say so.
Kofi looks at his hand and spreads his fingers wide. He knows that the same bones were once inside a fin, and he feels a new respect for his own body.
At last the hiccups stop, and Kofi says goodbye to Dr Adjoa. He walks out into the evening knowing that his body is a living museum of very old parts.
C1C2: Kofi had been hiccuping since lunchtime, and every hic bounced off the marble walls of the museum so loudly that people turned to stare. Dr Adjoa, the fossil scientist who had offered to show him around, only smiled and said that even a hiccup has a very old story hidden inside it. If he would follow her, she promised, they would spend the afternoon tracing the body he lives in back to its beginnings.

Standing beneath a skeleton so tall that it nearly touched the ceiling, Dr Adjoa explained that every animal with a backbone is a distant cousin of every other. Fish, frogs, snakes, birds, cats and children share ancestors who lived unimaginably long ago, and each group has simply inherited and altered a common set of parts. It is rather as if a very old family had spread across the world and kept some of its traits.

Kofi asked how anyone could possibly know what happened hundreds of millions of years before the first person was born. Dr Adjoa answered that scientists draw on several kinds of evidence at once, namely fossils, the bodies of living animals, the way embryos develop and the letters of DNA. When separate lines of evidence point to the same story, she added, it becomes very hard to doubt.

Dr Adjoa paused before a long shelf of birds and beetles to explain how this change happens, because it follows a simple pattern. Individuals in any group differ slightly, some of those differences are inherited, and the ones that help an animal to survive and reproduce become more common over many generations. No one is in charge and no goal is being pursued, she said, because the process simply works with whatever variation happens to be present.

Fossils are made when the hard parts of a dead animal are quickly buried in mud or sand, and minerals slowly seep in and turn them into stone. Rock builds up in layers over time, so the deeper layers are usually the older ones, and a fossil's place in the stack tells scientists roughly when it lived. It is a slow and uncommon process, which is why every fossil that survives is something of a small miracle.

Certain atoms found in rock are radioactive, which means that they change into other kinds of atom at a steady and well-measured rate. By comparing how much of the original atom remains with how much of its product has appeared, scientists can calculate how long ago the rock formed, much as one might read an hourglass. Rocks that lie above and below a fossil can therefore give it a surprisingly reliable age.

More than five hundred million years ago, in a sea that held no forests and no animals on land, the first creatures with something like a backbone appeared. They were small, slender and fish-like, with no jaws, no limbs and very little armour, and yet they carried the basic plan from which every later vertebrate would descend. If you could meet one of them, you would be meeting a distant grandparent of every person alive today.

Kofi reached around and felt the knobbly line of his spine through his shirt, and Dr Adjoa told him that this row of bones was an inheritance from the earliest fish. So was the skull that guards his brain, for the basic arrangement of a backbone at the back and a protective case at the front goes back to those distant swimmers. Over time the design was altered and refined, but it was never thrown away.

In the Fish Hall, a large skeleton of a fish had been placed beside that of a human, and Kofi was startled by how many features they shared. Both had a skull at one end, a long spine running behind, and curved ribs enclosing the middle, even though the fish had fins where the person had arms and legs. The similarities were not coincidences, Dr Adjoa said, but the marks of a shared inheritance.

In a glass tank, Dr Adjoa showed Kofi a lamprey, a long, eel-like fish with a round, toothed mouth like a funnel and no hinged jaw whatsoever. Lampreys are living relatives of the earliest jawless vertebrates, which makes them a useful window into how those ancient animals may have lived. They cannot bite as we do, but must hold fast to their food and scrape or suck it into their mouths.

A fish breathes by passing water over its gills, thin and feathery organs that absorb the oxygen dissolved in the water. Each gill is supported by a curved bar of bone or cartilage called a gill arch, and a row of these arches lines each side of the throat like the ribs of a small boat. Hold on to that image, Dr Adjoa said, because those bars are about to become very important.

Over a vast stretch of time, the front pair of gill arches in some early fish changed, growing larger and stronger until they formed hinged jaws that could open and close. This was an enormous advantage, because an animal that can bite and chew can eat a much wider range of food than one that can only filter or suck. Jawed fish spread through the seas, and every jawed animal alive today, including you, descends from them.

The skin of a shark feels like sandpaper, because it is covered in thousands of tiny, tooth-shaped scales called denticles, which are made of much the same materials as teeth. Many scientists think that teeth began as scales of this kind, and that they gradually moved from the skin into the mouth of early jawed fish. The enamel that you brush twice a day may therefore have started life as a kind of armour on the outside of an ancient body.

The skeleton of a shark is made not of bone but of cartilage, the firm and flexible material that you can feel if you bend the tip of your nose or the rim of your ear. Cartilage is also what much of a human baby's skeleton consists of before birth, and over time a large part of it is slowly replaced by hard bone. Sharks, in other words, have kept a stage that we pass through as we grow.

Not long after a human embryo begins to grow, a series of small ridges and grooves appears along the sides of its neck, and these are called pharyngeal arches. They are not gills and never breathe water, but in the embryos of fish they develop into just that, whereas in people they are reshaped into pieces of the jaw, the ear and the throat. It is a vivid example of an old developmental pattern being reused for new purposes.

The human heart begins its life as a plain tube that has just started to pulse, and over the following weeks it bends, loops and divides into separate chambers. A fish heart has only two chambers, one to receive blood and one to push it out, and the more complicated hearts of other animals are variations on that theme. Each stage in our heart's development, though, is a growth stage and not a replay of any particular ancestor.

Across the main groups of vertebrates, the heart gains complexity in steps, from the two chambers of a fish to the three of a frog and the four of a mammal or a bird. The separate chambers on the right and left keep blood that is rich in oxygen from mixing with blood that has already been used, which suits the high energy needs of a warm-blooded body. Evolution seldom starts again from nothing, and it modified the old design bit by bit.

In a fish, a nerve runs from the brain to each of the gill arches. In people, several major nerves of the head and neck still follow routes that match the old pattern, although the jaw, throat and facial muscles they serve have changed beyond recognition. The wiring, in other words, still remembers the plan of the original house, however much the rooms have changed.

One nerve that serves the voice box, the laryngeal nerve, leaves the brain, runs all the way down a giraffe's long neck, loops beneath a large blood vessel near the heart, and then travels back up to the throat. The detour is several metres long and seems absurd until you remember that in the ancestors of fish this route was short and direct, passing behind a gill arch. As the neck stretched, the nerve was lengthened with it, because evolution does not rewire from scratch.

It is tempting to think that lungs were invented for life on land, but they appeared much earlier in some early bony fish, which gulped air to supplement the oxygen from their gills. The swim bladder that helps many modern fish float is not the ancestor of lungs at all, but a later modification of them, a remarkable change of purpose from breathing to buoyancy. Our own lungs, then, belong to a very old tradition that began in the water.

In a murky pool at the back of the Fish Hall floated a lungfish, a living species that breathes air through true lungs as well as through gills. Some of them can survive for months in dried mud by curling up and breathing air, which gives a lively idea of how fish with similar abilities might have coped when their pools shrank. Dr Adjoa pointed out that such creatures show how the first step towards land may have been small and practical.

Along each side of a fish runs a faint line of tiny sensors, each with microscopic hairs that bend when the water moves around the body, which tells the animal about currents and about neighbours swimming nearby. The cells in your inner ear that detect sound and keep you balanced use hairs in a very similar way, and they are close relatives of the fish's sensors. It is a good example of an old tool being used for a new job.

Deep inside each ear, behind the bone of the skull, are three small loops filled with fluid that let the brain know when the head turns or tilts. A very similar arrangement exists in fish and in almost all other animals with backbones, which shows that this balancing organ is extremely ancient and has been successfully kept. Kofi decided that he would be a little more grateful the next time he spun around and did not fall over.

The early ancestors of vertebrates had four types of cone, the cells in the eye that detect colour, so their view of the world may have been richer than ours. Early mammals, which lived mostly in the dark, lost two of those types, and only some of the primates later regained a third by a change in an existing gene. That is why we see a good range of colours, although a bee or a goldfish might look at us and see a rather dull picture.

Human noses use about four hundred working genes to build the receptors that detect smells, whereas a mouse has more than a thousand. Our genomes still contain the remains of hundreds of others that are now broken and silent, a trace of a time when scent mattered more to our ancestors than sight. Even so, scientists have found that people can distinguish an enormous range of odours, so the loss of those genes was by no means a disaster.

Inside a fleshy fin of an ancient fish lie bones arranged in a clear pattern, with one large bone nearest the body, two bones next, and then a collection of smaller ones. Your arm has been built in the same sequence, with the single humerus in the upper arm, the radius and ulna in the forearm and a cluster of wrist and finger bones at the end. The same structure serves the wing of a bat, the flipper of a whale and the leg of a horse.

Kofi wanted to know why any fish would trade the sea for the land, and Dr Adjoa said that scientists still discuss the answer. At the time, plants and insects were already living along the shore, and the warm shallow pools where fish lived could be crowded, full of predators and short of oxygen. A fish that could haul itself through the mud for a short way might find food and safety that its neighbours could not reach.

Tiktaalik was a fish about as long as a small crocodile that lived in shallow waters some 375 million years ago, and its fossils have been found in the Arctic of Canada. It had gills and scales like a fish, but also a flat head with eyes on top, ribs that were sturdy enough to support its body and fins that contained wrist-like joints. Scientists describe it as a transitional form, a creature that shows features of both groups at once.

Most fish have no neck, because their head is attached directly to the shoulder bones, so they must turn the entire body in order to look sideways. Tiktaalik had a neck in the true sense, which let it move its head independently of the rest of its body, and that would have been valuable when stalking prey in the shallows. When you nod or glance over your shoulder, you are using a freedom that began in creatures like this.

The earliest tetrapods, animals with four limbs and fingers, appear in the fossil record about 365 million years ago, and many of them were still creatures of the water. One of these, Acanthostega, had limbs that were not strong enough to carry it for long on land, and it had eight fingers on each hand instead of five. The first limbs, then, were probably paddles used in swamps and shallow pools, and they were only later turned into legs for walking.

Early four-limbed animals tried out several numbers of fingers and toes, including seven and eight, and only later did the pattern of five become the usual one among their descendants. Many animals later lost some of them, as a horse has done, but none seem to have added new ones. Your own hand, with its five fingers, thus bears the marks of a pattern that was chosen long ago and then kept.

A group of genes called the Hox genes acts like a set of address labels along the length of an embryo, telling each region whether it should become a head, a chest or a tail. Remarkably, flies, fish, mice and people all use closely related sets of Hox genes for the same job, which implies that they were inherited from a distant common ancestor. Changes in how they are switched on can help to explain how bodies with the same basic plan end up so different.

The zebrafish is a tiny freshwater fish that has become a favourite in laboratories, partly because about seven in ten human genes have a recognisable counterpart in its genome. Its embryos are also transparent, so researchers can watch the heart, the blood vessels and the nerves develop in a living animal under a microscope. What they learn about these small striped fish often helps them to understand human health and disease.

A gene known as Pax6 has an important role in starting the development of eyes in animals as different as insects, fish and mammals, and the versions in different species are similar enough that scientists can swap them. The compound eye of a fly and the camera-like eye of a person are built in very different ways and probably evolved separately, yet an old genetic switch seems to be common to them both. It is another case of evolution reusing a tool that was already in the box.

A frog's life story reads like a short history of vertebrates moving onto land, for it begins as a tadpole with gills and a tail and ends as an adult that breathes with lungs and absorbs air through its skin. Amphibians must still return to the water to lay their jelly-covered eggs, because the eggs would dry out in the air. They show how the first land animals may have remained tied to the water for a long time.

A later step in the move onto land was the evolution of an egg with a waterproof shell and several protective membranes, which could be laid on dry ground without drying out. Animals that hatch from such eggs, the reptiles, birds and mammals, are called amniotes, and they no longer needed ponds in which to breed. Humans are descended from this line, which is why a mammal embryo still grows inside a membrane, the amnion, filled with watery fluid.

A reptile's lower jaw is made up of several separate bones, whereas the jaw of a mammal consists of just one, which gave scientists a puzzle to solve. The fossils of creatures that lived before and during the rise of the mammals showed that, over millions of years, the smaller bones at the back of the jaw shrank and became less and less involved in chewing. They were gradually drawn into a brand new role, forming a delicate connection with the ear.

Behind the eardrum, in the middle ear, sit the three smallest bones in the body, the hammer, the anvil and the stirrup, which pass vibrations from the drum to the inner ear. Two of them, the hammer and the anvil, were once part of the jaw joint in the reptile-like ancestors of mammals, and fossils and embryos both show them moving from one job to the other. It is one of the clearest stories in all of anatomy, and Dr Adjoa clearly loved it.

In the diorama of the mammal hall, a furry mother lay curled around her young while they drank her milk, and Dr Adjoa observed that these two traits define the mammals. Hair keeps a warm-blooded body warm, and milk lets a mother feed her babies without having to find the right food for them, and both features seem to have arisen in small early relatives of ours. Your own hair and the milk you drank as an infant are gifts from a very old line.

When Kofi shivered in the cool air of the Hall of Mammals, a tiny muscle at the base of each hair on his arm pulled it upright and raised little bumps on his skin. In furry animals, the same reflex fluffs up the coat to trap warm air or to make the creature look larger to a rival, but our sparse body hair means that it does almost nothing for us. It is a small, harmless leftover of a time when our ancestors were much hairier.

At last they came back to Kofi's hiccups, which the fresh air of the hall had not cured. Some scientists have suggested that hiccuping is the remains of an old reflex that helps tadpoles and other gill-breathing animals to pump water, closing the throat at just the right moment. Dr Adjoa was quick to say that nobody has proved this, and that the true reason for hiccups remains an open question.

Early in pregnancy, a human embryo has a short tail that contains small bones. It gradually shrinks and disappears, and the only trace left at birth is the coccyx, a small cluster of fused bones at the lower end of the spine. This so-called tailbone still has a use, since it serves as an anchor for muscles and ligaments, but it also remains as a record of our ancestry.

Animals that lay eggs make a rich yolk to feed the growing embryo, using proteins that are coded by a small family of genes. The human genome contains a damaged copy of one of these genes, a silent fragment that was left behind after the mammals began feeding their young in the womb and with milk instead. Such a broken gene is a little like a page torn from an old cookbook that is no longer used but has never been thrown away.

The human spine began as a design for animals that walked and swam in a horizontal position, and it was gradually modified for walking upright on two legs. The result is remarkably good, yet it is a compromise, and many scientists think that the aches in our backs and knees are partly the price of using an old structure in a new way. Evolution does not aim for perfection, because it works only with what is already there.

In your throat, the path for air and the path for food cross, so that every swallow must be carefully timed to keep the food out of the windpipe. This inconvenient design arises because the lungs began as a pocket budding from the gut of early vertebrates, so the airway never had a separate entrance of its own. It is why people can choke, and it is a small price for a body that was adapted, not designed from scratch.

In the nineteenth century, a German scientist named Ernst Haeckel published drawings of embryos that exaggerated their similarity, and he claimed that each animal re-enacts its ancestors' history as it develops. Later scientists showed that his drawings were misleading and his idea was wrong, and yet the early stages of embryos do share real features, such as the neck arches, which reflect the common ancestry. Careful modern research thus keeps what is true, discards what is not and keeps checking both.

Dr Adjoa led Kofi to a huge branching diagram on the wall that showed how all vertebrates are related, from the oldest fish to the newest mammals. One tree was built by comparing the shapes of bones and fossils, and another was built by comparing the letters of DNA, and the two agree on most of the main branches. When two entirely independent methods give the same answer, scientists regard it as strong support for the picture.

Every year, fossil hunters working in deserts, cliffs and quarries all over the world uncover new specimens, and each of them can add a new detail to the story or force scientists to change an old one. There are still gaps and disagreements, for example about exactly which fish were our closest relatives, and honest scientists say so openly. This readiness to be corrected is the very thing that makes science so reliable.

Kofi spread his fingers wide and turned his hand over in the light of the museum window, as though he were seeing it for the first time. Inside it were the bones of an ancient fin, rearranged over hundreds of millions of years into something that could grip a pencil, throw a ball and hold a friend's hand. He felt a strange new respect for the body he had always taken for granted.

As the museum prepared to close, Kofi noticed with surprise that his hiccups had quietly stopped, and he thanked Dr Adjoa for a wonderful afternoon. He walked out into the golden evening light with the strong sense that he was carrying a living museum inside him, filled with parts that had been inherited, reused and altered across a gulf of time. Each one, from the bones in his ears to the hiccup that had begun the day, had a story that he now knew how to begin to tell.
